summary:
Most people learn space one fact at a time. Real missions don’t work that way.

SpaceBnB puts you in the chair of a mission designer. Pick a mission, such as watching wildfires from orbit. Identify your budget, choose an orbit and a rocket, then build your spacecraft from component cards. Every card costs something somewhere else: a sharper camera eats mass, power, data and money.

Then space pushes back. A solar array refuses to unfold. A storm of radiation rolls in. Debris drifts into your path. The cards you built decide which counters you hold, so every design choice comes back to meet you in flight.

At the end, a report names the exact decision that cost you the mission.

Inspired by real NASA missions, written in plain language for anyone 13 and up, and different on every run, Mission Control doesn’t tell you how space missions work. It lets you find out.
details:
Overview

SpaceBnB is a space mission card game that lets players design, test, launch and operate a complete mission. Existing learning tools usually teach one topic at a time, such as orbital mechanics, spacecraft design or rocket launches. A real mission is a system where every decision limits another. We built a game where those links are the gameplay.

What it does and how it works

A run follows the real mission process through five stages.

1. Define the mission. The player picks a mission. Each comes with a briefing that explains the real-world need, the user it serves and the NASA mission that inspired it. The player then draws objectives, rolls a random budget within the mission’s cost range, and picks a duration.

2. Set the segments. The player chooses an orbit, a launch vehicle and a ground segment. These form the board, the rules the spacecraft must live with. Every option leads with one plain sentence of meaning, such as “sees the whole planet in steady morning light.”

3. Build and test. The player chooses a spacecraft bus and fills its slots with component cards from a hangar. A component card has two jobs. It must fit the mission, meaning its mass, power, cost and ability tags must meet what the objectives need. It also produces action cards for the flight deck. A good part adds helpful actions. A cheap, less reliable part adds negative “glitch” cards that fire the moment they are drawn. A preflight dashboard shows mass, power, delta-v, data in versus data out, lifetime and cost, with warnings and an objective check. A test campaign then reveals some of the hazards that are coming, and a counter check shows which ones the player’s deck can answer.

4. Launch and operate. A launch roll is made against the vehicle’s reliability. The mission then flies five phases: launch, early operations, two operations phases and an extended phase. In each phase the player reads a hazard and its impact, such as a solar array that fails to latch, a debris conjunction or a solar particle storm. The player draws and plays action cards that match the hazard’s threat. Cards are kept between turns and used up when played, so the real choice is whether to play a card now or hold it for later.

5. Evaluate. The game gives an ending, from Launch Failure to Outstanding Success, and a score out of 100 with a grade. The core of the report is a cause-and-effect trace. Each lost point is linked to one decision and a suggested fix. For example: “Sharp Eyes missed: your imager gives 21 m/px at 700 km; the goal is 5 m.”

Benefits

  • It shows the whole journey. Players walk through every stage and gain an overview of how a mission is planned and flown.
  • It makes constraints felt. Budget, mass, power, data, communications and time limit one another. A better instrument adds mass, power, data and cost, and the player sees that before reading about it.
  • It rewards strategy. Players decide what to build, what to hold and when to play. They learn while having fun.
  • It is grounded in real missions. Missions, cost classes and hazards are inspired by actual NASA projects.
  • It is accessible. Plain language, an explanation for every detail and a final report mean a beginner can play and understand.
  • It is replayable. The budget, objectives, hazards and card draws are random. The build itself has no luck, so the randomness tests the design rather than the player.

Intended impact

We want more people to understand that space missions succeed through integrated engineering decisions, not through isolated facts. The game is aimed at students aged 13 and up and at anyone curious about space, especially those with little prior knowledge. We hope players leave with three things: an intuition for trade-offs, the vocabulary of real mission design, and the confidence to keep exploring. Because failure is safe and explained, players are encouraged to try again and improve their design.

Tools and technologies

  • Languages and frameworks: TypeScript, React, plan CSS.
  • State management: useReducer over pure engine reducers (state, input) -> state
  • Hosting: GitHub Pages via GitHub Actions
  • Art and sound: CC0 sprites from Kenney, the Press Start 2P font and browser-generated retro sound effects.

What makes it creative

  • A mission as a card game. The usual way to teach engineering is a simulator or a quiz. We turned the build into a deck. Your spacecraft decides your hand, so design and gameplay are the same thing.
  • Components that do two jobs. Each card must fit the numbers and also creates the actions that defend the mission later. That makes “what you pick” and “what you can do” one idea.
  • Glitches as the price of cheap parts. Low-reliability parts add negative cards to the deck. Players feel the cost of saving money without a lecture.
  • A report that teaches. Instead of a bare score, the game explains the cause of each loss and what to try next.
  • Real history in the hazards. Each hazard echoes a real event, such as a solar array that did not fully latch or a high-gain antenna that never opened, so players connect the game to real missions.
